evidence.claim: At the June 2022 TPNW states-parties meeting in Vienna, Thailand said the treaty complements existing disarmament and nonproliferation mechanisms and took part in planning the treaty’s intersessional structure.
evidence.title: Permanent Secretary for Foreign Affairs reaffirmed Thailand’s commitment towards the achievement of a World Free of Nuclear Weapons at the First Meeting of States Parties to the TPNW
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.excerpt: At the June 2022 TPNW states-parties meeting in Vienna, Thailand said the treaty complements existing disarmament and nonproliferation mechanisms and took part in planning the treaty’s intersessional structure.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official Thai MFA statement with a precise 2022 date and explicit treaty-policy content.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to Thailand’s nuclear-disarmament posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is attributable to the Thai foreign-policy apparatus under Prayut’s government, not to a personal nuclear command decision.
contrary_evidence: The statement is multilateral and diplomatic; it does not show operational control over any nuclear capability.

evidence.claim: Thailand hosted the April 2022 ARF nonproliferation meeting and emphasized the NPT pillars, Bangkok Treaty implementation, TPNW complementarity, peaceful nuclear uses with safety/security/safeguards, and cooperation on technological innovations and emerging technologies.
evidence.title: Thailand hosted the 13th ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) Inter-Sessional Meeting on Non-Proliferation and Disarmament (ISM on NPD)
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.excerpt: Thailand hosted the April 2022 ARF nonproliferation meeting and emphasized the NPT pillars, Bangkok Treaty implementation, TPNW complementarity, peaceful nuclear uses with safety/security/safeguards, and cooperation on technological innovations and emerging technologies.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official MFA summary of a dated 2022 multilateral meeting with specific policy priorities.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to chapters 1B, 4B, and 8B as institutional context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Thailand’s foreign-policy leadership under Prayut’s government, not to a personal nuclear command action.
contrary_evidence: This is agenda-setting and coordination, not proof of enhanced command-and-control or crisis restraint.

evidence.claim: Thailand’s official nuclear-safety agency says the CTBT bans all nuclear explosions, Thailand signed in 1996 and ratified in 2018, and the country operates CTBT monitoring stations and a national data center.
evidence.title: สนธิสัญญาว่าด้วยการห้ามทดลองนิวเคลียร์โดยสมบูรณ์ (Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty: CTBT)
evidence.publisher: Office of Atoms for Peace, Thailand
evidence.excerpt: Thailand’s official nuclear-safety agency says the CTBT bans all nuclear explosions, Thailand signed in 1996 and ratified in 2018, and the country operates CTBT monitoring stations and a national data center.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Thai official source with explicit treaty history and the monitoring infrastructure located in Thailand.
evidence.period_fit: Stable background for 2022 civil monitoring and nuclear-test prohibition.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to state institutions under Prayut’s government, not to personal nuclear command authority.
contrary_evidence: The page describes civil monitoring and treaty compliance; it does not show a unique 2022 ruler decision.

evidence.claim: The TPNW prohibits use, threat of use, possession, testing, transfer, stationing, and related assistance; Thailand is listed as a ratified party, and each party must keep existing IAEA safeguards.
evidence.title: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW)
evidence.excerpt: The TPNW prohibits use, threat of use, possession, testing, transfer, stationing, and related assistance; Thailand is listed as a ratified party, and each party must keep existing IAEA safeguards.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent treaty reference with explicit status and compliance language; not an official registry, but detailed and stable.
evidence.period_fit: Useful baseline and interpretive framework for Thailand’s 2022 treaty posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The treaty position is state-level and inherited; it does not by itself show Prayut’s direct hand on existential-risk policy.
contrary_evidence: NTI notes that the treaty lacks its own verification regime and relies on existing IAEA safeguards.

evidence.claim: The NPT is the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation regime, aimed at preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear energy, and requiring IAEA safeguards for non-nuclear-weapon states.
evidence.title: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT)
evidence.publisher: United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs
evidence.excerpt: The NPT is the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation regime, aimed at preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear energy, and requiring IAEA safeguards for non-nuclear-weapon states.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN disarmament reference for the treaty’s role and safeguards architecture.
evidence.period_fit: Foundational background for Thailand’s 2022 treaty posture and regional nonproliferation commitments.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is global treaty structure, not a Prayut-specific action.
contrary_evidence: The page describes the regime framework, not Thailand-specific implementation quality.

evidence.claim: Thai Research Reactor-1/Modification 1 was used for radioisotope production, nuclear technology research and education, and Thailand’s safety procedures required health-physics oversight and radiation-control checks.
evidence.title: Radiation Safety Management Regulation of Thai Research Reactor-1/Modification 1 for Reactor Health Physicist Implementation
evidence.publisher: International Atomic Energy Agency conference platform
evidence.excerpt: Thai Research Reactor-1/Modification 1 was used for radioisotope production, nuclear technology research and education, and Thailand’s safety procedures required health-physics oversight and radiation-control checks.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: IAEA conference abstract from a Thai nuclear-institution speaker; specific but narrower than a full inspection report.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and useful for showing Thailand’s civil-nuclear, safety-governed exposure rather than a weapons posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional civil-nuclear management, not a Prayut personal command decision.
contrary_evidence: A research reactor is not a nuclear weapon capability; this is safety context, not existential-risk leadership proof.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 ruler-attributed existential-risk choice, escalation, or crisis-management episode is shown.
Command-and-control, custody, and safety-governance evidence tied specifically to Prayut remains thin.
PM-level attribution for 2022 international-security choices is still thin; most evidence is ministry or delegation posture.
The Myanmar and Ukraine material does not yet show concrete peace or accountability outcomes attributable to Prayut.
Direct chain-of-command evidence for the APEC crackdown and the deep-south emergency regime remains limited.
The torture/disappearance law is an important reform, but year-end enforcement evidence is still weak.
Direct evidence on the sponsors and mechanism of the election-system change is still thin.
4B.4 and 4B.7 remain under-evidenced relative to the stronger protest, media, and term-limit material.
Budget intent and macro recovery are better evidenced than actual implementation and take-up.
Evidence on appointments, anti-capture, and mistake-correction is still weak.
Direct service-delivery, take-up, and quality evidence is thin outside budget allocations and national surveys.
Ruler-specific causal attribution for rural, child, and mental-health outcomes remains weak.
No independent 2022 finding of personal lying, self-dealing, or concealed conflict of interest is shown.
The package relies too much on allegations, self-defense, and broader regime context.
The program basis is only partly explicit; some objectives are inferred from budgets and coalition moves rather than a single frozen program statement.
Outcome evidence is sectoral and mixed, and external reopening effects remain hard to separate from ruler skill.
